```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise:
#|  - nn-data
#|  - nn-model
#|  - nn-predict
#|  - nn-experiment

library(readr)
library(nnet)
library(dplyr)

esol <- read_csv("data/esol_clean.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

set.seed(42)

# Select descriptors
esol_nn <- esol %>%
  select(`Molecular Weight`, `Number of H-Bond Donors`, `Polar Surface Area`,
         `measured log solubility in mols per litre`)

# Simple train-test split
train_index <- sample(seq_len(nrow(esol_nn)), size = 0.7 * nrow(esol_nn))
train <- esol_nn[train_index, ]
test <- esol_nn[-train_index, ]

nn_model <- nnet(
  `measured log solubility in mols per litre` ~ `Molecular Weight` + `Number of H-Bond Donors` + `Polar Surface Area`,
  data = train,
  size = 3,       # hidden neurons
  linout = TRUE,  # regression output
  trace = FALSE
)

```

### What is a Neural Network?

Neural networks are machine learning models inspired by the brain. They can detect complex patterns in data by combining inputs in layers of connected “neurons.”

For our chemical dataset:

 - **Inputs**: molecular descriptors such as `molecular weight`, `number of h bond donors`, `polar surface area`
 - **Hidden layer**: neurons that learn combinations of these features
 - **Output**: predicted property (e.g. solubility)

::: callback-note
Each neuron sums its inputs, applies a simple transformation, and passes the result to the next layer.
:::

### [WebR]{.tag-webr} Preparing the Data

We’ll predict solubility using a few descriptors. First, split the dataset into training and testing sets as we did previously in Workshop 7. If this approach doesn't look familiar to you, please review thre previous workshop.

```{webr}
#| exercise: nn-data

set.seed(42)

# Select descriptors
esol_nn <- esol %>%
  select(`Molecular Weight`, `Number of H-Bond Donors`, `Polar Surface Area`,
         `measured log solubility in mols per litre`)

# Simple train-test split
train_index <- sample(seq_len(nrow(esol_nn)), size = 0.7 * nrow(esol_nn))
train <- esol_nn[train_index, ]
test <- esol_nn[-train_index, ]

head(train)
str(train)
```

Here, the `select()` command enables us to pick the columns that we want from the dataset, while the `seq_len()` command generates a sequence of row numbers for the molecules.

[<strong>ACTIVITY:</strong>]{.highlight-green} Check the training set:

 - How many molecules are in the training set?
 - How many descriptors are we using?

### Building a Simple Neural Network

We will use the `nnet` package to build a simple network with one hidden layer of 3 neurons.

```{webr}

#| exercise: nn-model

set.seed(42)

nn_model <- nnet(
  `measured log solubility in mols per litre` ~ `Molecular Weight` + `Number of H-Bond Donors` + `Polar Surface Area`,
  data = train,
  size = 3,       # hidden neurons
  linout = TRUE,  # regression output
  trace = FALSE
)

nn_model
```

:::callback-note
The model has now learned patterns in the data, combining descriptors to approximate solubility.
:::

Descriptions of the commands used here are as follows:

 - `nn_model <- nnet(...)` → “Train a neural network and store it as nn_model.” Think of it like naming your robot that will predict solubility.
 - `measured_log_solubility_in_mols_per_litre ~ ...` → “I want to predict solubility using these descriptors.” The left side is the thing you want to predict, the right side are the ingredients you feed in.
 - `data = train` → “Use the training molecules to teach the network.”
`size = 3` → “Use 3 neurons in the hidden layer.” Each neuron is like a mini-brain that combines information from the descriptors.
 - `linout = TRUE` → “We’re predicting a number, not a category.”
 - `trace = FALSE` → “Don’t print a million messages while the network trains.”

### Making Predictions

```{webr}
#| exercise: nn-predict

test$prediction <- predict(nn_model, test)

ggplot(test, aes(x = `measured log solubility in mols per litre`, y = prediction)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue") +
  geom_abline(color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted vs Measured Solubility",
    x = "Measured log Solubility",
    y = "Predicted log Solubility"
  )
```

[<strong>ACTIVITY:</strong>]{.highlight-green} Review the neural network prediction above and decide whether it predicts solubility well? Are there molecules that are predicted poorly? Why might that happen?

[EXPERIMENT]{.highlight-pink} Try changing the number of hidden neurons in the code below from 3 to 5 or 7 and see how predictions change.

```{webr}
#| exercise: nn-experiment

# Modify size parameter
nn_model2 <- nnet(
  `measured log solubility in mols per litre` ~ `Molecular Weight` + `Number of H-Bond Donors` + `Polar Surface Area`,
  data = train,
  size = ____,   # try 5 or 7
  linout = TRUE,
  trace = FALSE
)

test$prediction2 <- predict(nn_model2, test)

ggplot(test, aes(x = `measured log solubility in mols per litre`, y = prediction2)) +
  geom_point(color = "green") +
  geom_abline(color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted vs Measured Solubility (Modified Network)"
  )
```

#### What happens when size = 3? (Very small network)

 - The network has only 3 hidden neurons to combine all inputs.
 - Each neuron can only learn a very limited set of patterns in the data.
 - *Result*: the network essentially averages the solubility for most molecules.

This is called **underfitting**: the model is too simple to capture the real relationships in the data.

Think of it as trying to paint a detailed landscape with only 3 crayons — you get the general shape, but no details.

#### Increasing size = 5 (small increase)

 - The network has more neurons, so it can start to learn some linear and slightly nonlinear patterns.
 - You see a loose correlation with actual solubility.
 - Still, the network is limited and cannot capture complex combinations of molecular weight, H-bond donors, and polar surface area.

Analogy: now you have 5 crayons — you can see rough shading and shapes, but the fine details are still missing.

#### Increasing size ≈ 50 (large network)

 - Now the network has enough capacity to model complex nonlinear relationships between descriptors and solubility.
 - It can combine features in many ways to approximate the observed values more accurately.
 - *Result*: predictions improve, correlation with measured solubility is much better.

Analogy: now you have 50 crayons — you can finally paint the details of the landscape accurately.

::: callback-warning
More neurons is NOT always better. With too many neurons relative to your dataset size, the network can overfit, meaning it memorizes training data but fails on new molecules. In this case, the ESOL dataset is only ~1128 molecules, so 50 neurons is probably fine, but 500 neurons would be risky!
:::

::: callback-note
In `nnet`, you can use the decay argument to penalize very large weights, which helps prevent overfitting in larger networks.
:::

### How Neural Networks Work Conceptually

Each descriptor is an input neuron... inputs are combined in hidden neurons using weighted sums. A nonlinear activation function allows the network to model complex relationships. Following this, the output neuron gives a predicted value. Even with just 3 inputs and 5 hidden neurons, the network can capture nonlinear relationships that a simple linear regression cannot.

```r
# Select descriptors

  select(`Molecular Weight`, `Number of H-Bond Donors`, `Polar Surface Area`,
         `measured log solubility in mols per litre`)

# Split train/test
set.seed(42)
train_index <- sample(seq_len(nrow(esol_nn)), size = 0.7 * nrow(esol_nn))
train <- esol_nn[train_index, ]
test <- esol_nn[-train_index, ]

# Build neural network
nn_model <- nnet(
  `measured log solubility in mols per litre` ~ `Molecular Weight` + `Number of H-Bond Donors` + `Polar Surface Area`,
  data = train,
  size = 5,
  linout = TRUE,
  trace = FALSE
)

# Predict and plot
test$prediction <- predict(nn_model, test)

ggplot(test, aes(x = `measured log solubility in mols per litre`, y = prediction)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue") +
  geom_abline(color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted vs Measured Solubility",
    x = "Measured log Solubility",
    y = "Predicted log Solubility"
  )
```
